A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same City-Networks study. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices are readable, allowing additions, revisions, and relocated material to be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification experiments, Jacobian-based influence measurements, and computational resource measurements in Sections 3–4 and Appendix B.

after.justification: v2 reports original classification and influence experiments, including expanded dataset comparisons and label-radius and model-width analyses in Appendices B–C.

M1.justification: Both versions retain the 37-feature construction, 16-hop road-length-based eccentricity labels divided into ten quantiles, and the same absolute-Jacobian aggregation and receptive-field measure R. v2 parameterizes the labeling radius as k and explains its selection without replacing the proposed procedure.

E1.justification: v2 adds Amazon-Ratings product-rating prediction and actual inductive PascalVOC-SP classification and influence evaluation. v1 used PascalVOC only for descriptive network comparisons. CiteSeer disappears from influence evaluation, while the four city networks, Cora, and ogbn-arxiv remain.

E2.justification: Compared with v1 Table 2, v2 Table 5 adds GAT, GCNII, DropEdge, GraphGPS, and Exphormer. ChebNet remains in that table but disappears from the depth and influence comparisons. The influence comparison adds GCNII, GraphGPS, and Exphormer; the fixed-depth ablation drops MLP and ChebNet and adds Exphormer.

E3.justification: The principal settings change from hidden size 32 and 20k epochs to hidden size 128 and up to 30k epochs. v2 introduces hyperparameter searches covering residual connections, normalization, dropout, and learning rate. City splits remain 10%/10%/80%. The new inductive influence evaluation averages over 100 sampled PascalVOC-SP test graphs.

E4.justification: v2 adds spatial-label case analyses, a Paris GCN experiment varying label radius across 8, 16, and 32, and hidden-width sweeps across three cities and four models. The existing fixed-depth, variable-hop analysis is retained and revised. v1's parameter-count, GPU-memory, and training/testing-time analyses are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report means and standard deviations over five runs. v2 Section 3 additionally specifies that these runs use different random seeds. The run count and uncertainty-reporting convention remain unchanged.

E6.justification: Many accuracy and influence results are replaced, alongside substantial new results. For example, GCN's Paris accuracy changes from 47.3±0.2 in v1 Table 2 to 53.2±0.3 in v2 Table 5, and its Paris R changes from 4.01 to 4.86. These accompany revised training settings and cannot establish same-setting improvements. New radius and width findings are also reported.

T1.justification: The cancellation proposition and proof change from opposing branches f(x) and -f(x) to separate node inputs with h_v=x_u-x_w (v1 Proposition 6.1; v2 Proposition G.1). The self-loop proposition now assumes more than two nodes, and dilution statements specify zero other influences. Most remaining mathematics is retained or relocated.

C1.justification: The central dataset, measurement, and theoretical contributions remain. The introduction broadens the empirical comparative claim from city-versus-social/citation networks to greater long-range dependence relative to heterophilic and existing inductive long-range benchmarks as well. This expands the claim's scope without introducing a different central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 explains how large-radius or exact eccentricity can become predictable from coordinates and why k=16 balances range, structural relevance, and memory demands. Appendix G.2 adds an interpretation of influence as individual sensitivity despite cancellation, and Appendix E identifies dense-graph computational limitations. The earlier tuning caveat is removed; the overlapping-neighborhood sampling limitation remains.

D1.justification: v2 documents PyTorch Geometric access to the dataset and measurement, changes training-code provenance, and specifies transformer backbones, omission of positional encoding, and hyperparameter search ranges/defaults. It also identifies hardware for Jacobian computation. Conversely, v1's full training-cluster description and detailed resource profiles are removed.

R1.justification: The introduction substantially expands positioning around heterophily and synthetic long-range benchmarks. Section 4 explicitly relates R to Bamberger et al. (2025), distinguishing per-hop influence diagnostics. Added urban-accessibility, tuning, and architectural literature further broadens the research context beyond v1's primarily citation-network and LRGB framing.

P1.justification: The introduction, dataset rationale, and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Section 2 is reorganized around research challenges, topology, and accessibility. Much theoretical exposition moves into Appendices F–H, the fixed-depth analysis moves into Appendix C, and the appendix hierarchy is substantially reorganized. A dedicated availability section is added.

P2.justification: Table 1 is transposed, benchmark and influence plots are expanded and redrawn, and the accuracy table gains model-family grouping and moves to the appendix. New multi-radius maps, a PascalVOC example, and radius/width plots replace the earlier resource plots. The fixed-depth plot is relocated and redrawn as v2 Figure 10.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central benchmark justification through direct heterophilic and LRGB comparisons, broader architectures, tuning, and width/radius controls (Sections 3–4 and Appendices B–C). These address v1's narrow empirical comparisons and acknowledged fixed-hyperparameter limitation. Dataset-access information also improves usability. Removing resource profiles reduces computational transparency, and sampling overlap remains unresolved, but the stronger validation provides a substantial overall gain.
